title: The LMU OSC GitHub Organization

## Overview

A **GitHub Organization** is a shared workspace where several people collaborate on repositories under a single umbrella. Unlike a personal account, the repositories belong to the group rather than to one person --- which gives us continuity when people leave, permissions we can manage in groups through teams, and one place ([github.com/lmu-osc](https://github.com/lmu-osc)) where all of our code, content, and documentation lives.

**This page documents only what is specific to the LMU OSC:** our teams, our permission defaults, and our onboarding and offboarding procedures. GitHub's own documentation is the reference for how GitHub's features work, and we link to it throughout. The pattern is always:

1. Read the linked GitHub documentation for the feature or task.
2. Come back here for the conventions and decisions *we* have made about it.

---

## What is a GitHub Organization?

An organization is effectively a **shared account** that several people belong to. Because the repositories belong to the group, they survive staff changes, and access can be managed in groups rather than person by person. Ours is at [github.com/lmu-osc](https://github.com/lmu-osc).

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [About organizations](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/collaborating-with-groups-in-organizations/about-organizations) explains personal accounts versus organizations in full --- then come back here for how ours is set up.

### What you'll see at github.com/lmu-osc

- **Pinned repositories** --- a few key repos at the top, such as this manual.
- **Organization README** --- a short description of who we are, taken from our `.github` repository.
- **Tabs** --- **Repositories**, **Packages**, and **People** are the ones you'll use. The Repositories tab lists everything we have (public ones to everyone, private ones only if you have access).

---

## Repositories

We keep a mix of **public** and **private** repositories:

- **Public** --- visible to anyone on the internet. All of our content repositories (this manual, our tutorials, our public-facing websites) are public, in line with our commitment to open science: anyone can view, clone, and learn from them.
- **Private** --- visible only to members with access. We use these for internal tools, drafts not yet ready for release, and configurations that contain sensitive information.

Work that shouldn't live in the shared GitHub organization --- internal server administration, for example --- goes to our organization on the **LRZ GitLab** instance instead: see [LRZ GitLab](/lrz-gitlab/index.qmd).

For what each of our main repositories is for, see [Repositories of the LMU Open Science Center](/github/our-repositories.qmd).

### Finding repositories

Browse the **Repositories** tab to see everything we have, and use the search bar there to filter by name, description, or topic. If you work on a repository regularly, star it so it's quick to find again.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Searching for repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-for-repositories) covers the search syntax in detail --- then come back here for how we organize ours.

If you can't find something, ask a staff member: it may be private and you may not have access yet, or it may be on LRZ GitLab.

## Organization features

GitHub provides several features at the organization level. Here's how we use (and don't use) them at the OSC.

### Teams

Teams are the primary way we manage permissions. Instead of adding people to individual repositories one by one, you can create a team, give that team a set of permissions across all repos (or specific ones), and then add or remove members from the team. This makes it easy to see who has access to what and to onboard or offboard people quickly.

Anyone who is an organization member but **not** in any team has only the organization's base permissions --- see [Base member permissions](#base-member-permissions).

#### How team permissions work

When you add someone to a team, they get that team's permission level --- its **repository role** --- on all repositories the team can access. From least to most access:

| Role | Can... |
|---|---|
| **Read** | View and clone, open issues, comment, review pull requests, send pull requests from forks |
| **Triage** | Read, plus labels, milestones, closing and assigning issues, and requesting reviews |
| **Write** | Triage, plus push branches and merge pull requests |
| **Maintain** | Write, plus repository configuration that doesn't change access or visibility |
| **Admin** | Everything, including repository settings, access, secrets, and destructive actions |

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Repository roles for an organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-repository-roles/repository-roles-for-an-organization) has the exhaustive permission matrix for each role --- then come back here for which roles our teams use.

> **Owner** is a separate, *organization*-level role rather than a repository role --- see [Organization owners](#organization-owners).

#### Our current teams

| Team | Who's in it | Access |
|---|---|---|
| `osc-admin-members` | Full-time staff | **Admin** on all repos, including CI/CD workflows and repository settings |
| `osc-research-assistants` | Student research assistants (HiWis) | **Admin** on all repos |
| `osc-trusted-members` | Non-staff, non-HiWi OSC members | **Maintain** on all repos |

- **`osc-admin-members`** --- full-time staff. In the future we may give staff their repository permissions through this team rather than through Owner status, to keep the number of Owners small.
- **`osc-research-assistants`** --- HiWis. Currently the same **Admin** access as staff, because HiWis work across many repositories and often need to manage settings and CI/CD workflows, not just push code.
- **`osc-trusted-members`** --- OSC members who are neither staff nor HiWis but should still be able to work across all of our repositories. **Maintain** is a step down from Admin, but in practice enough for reviewing code, managing issues, and coordinating releases.

> **Repository Admin is not the same as being an organization Owner.** Our teams have Admin on the repositories, which is what lets them manage code, workflows, and repository settings --- but only Owners can invite or remove members or change organization-wide settings. See [Who can do what](#who-can-do-what).

#### Creating a new team

Any member can create a team, unless the owners have restricted team creation. Check the [organization role management settings](https://github.com/organizations/lmu-osc/settings/org_roles) first, and follow the principle of least privilege: **start with Read or Write** unless there's a clear need for Admin, since it's easier to escalate permissions later than to roll them back after an accident. Giving the team access to repositories needs admin access to those repositories --- ask a staff member if you don't have it.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [About teams](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/organizing-members-into-teams/about-teams) and [Creating a team](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/organizing-members-into-teams/creating-a-team).

#### Practical example: onboarding and offboarding a HiWi

When a new student research assistant joins, a staff member does the following:

1. **Invite them to the organization**, adding them to the `osc-research-assistants` team in the same step --- see [Adding new members](#adding-new-members) below.
2. **They accept the invitation** and automatically get Admin access to all repositories.

**When they leave**, the offboarding steps are:

1. **A staff member (or a maintainer of that team) removes them from the `osc-research-assistants` team.** This is the step that actually revokes their elevated access --- it takes effect across every repository at once, so you don't have to hunt down individual permissions.
2. **A staff member decides whether they should stay in the organization.** This is a judgement call:
   - If they're leaving the OSC entirely (contract or studies finished, no ongoing collaboration), **remove them from the organization** as well --- again an owner-level action. They then have no access at all.
   - If they'll stay connected --- for example as an alumni contact, a co-author, or an occasional collaborator --- **keep them as a member** but out of the team. They then fall back to the base permissions (Read): they can still browse and clone our repositories and take part in discussions, but they can no longer push to them.

> **Tip:** Removing someone from a team is reversible and cheap; removing them from the organization (and re-inviting them later) is not. If you're unsure, take them out of the team first --- you can always remove their membership later.

### Discussions

We use Discussions for **forum-style conversations** that aren't tied to a specific issue or pull request. So far we've only adopted them for the [main OSC website](https://github.com/lmu-osc/lmu-osc.github.io/discussions), which holds a backlog of ideas for the site; otherwise we rely on **Issues** for tracking tasks and bugs and **pull requests** for proposing and reviewing changes. If a topic doesn't have a clear actionable issue yet --- a design proposal, say --- feel free to start a discussion.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [GitHub Discussions](https://docs.github.com/en/discussions).

### Projects

Projects are GitHub's **Kanban-style boards**. We experimented with them and found they didn't fit our workflow, so we don't use them formally at the organization level --- but you're welcome to create your own for personal productivity: a board for issues you're responsible for, a fixed-timeline event, or a short-term initiative. Just don't expect others to use or maintain it.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [About Projects](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/planning-and-tracking-with-projects/learning-about-projects/about-projects).

## Membership and permissions

There are four kinds of people in our organization's ecosystem:

- **Base member** --- a member who isn't in any team, so the organization's base permission is all they have: they can clone and read everything and contribute through forks, but they cannot push to our repositories. See [Base member permissions](#base-member-permissions).
- **Member** --- a normal organization member; appears in the member list and counts toward any license seats.
- **Owner** --- a member with full control over the organization. We reserve this for full-time staff --- see [Organization owners](#organization-owners).
- **Outside collaborator** --- not a member at all; granted direct access to specific repositories only, and never appears in the member list.

Members and outside collaborators differ in more than permissions: members can be organized into teams and can see the organization as a whole, whereas outside collaborators only see the repositories they've been added to. As a rule, **members** are for people working with us over time, and **outside collaborators** for one-off or narrowly scoped work.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Roles in an organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-peoples-access-to-your-organization-with-roles/roles-in-an-organization) and [Adding outside collaborators to repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-outside-collaborators/adding-outside-collaborators-to-repositories-in-your-organization).

### Who can do what

Several of the tasks described below need a specific role. In our organization **Owners are full-time staff**, while both staff and HiWis have **Admin on every repository** through their teams. Team membership gives repository access, not organization ownership.

| Task | Who can do it |
|---|---|
| Invite someone to the organization | An organization **owner** (staff). A **team maintainer** can also invite a non-member directly into their team, which sends the same invitation. |
| Add an existing member to a team | An organization **owner**, or a **maintainer** of that team |
| Remove someone from the organization | An organization **owner** (staff) |
| Remove someone from a team | An organization **owner**, or a **maintainer** of that team |
| Add an outside collaborator to a repository | Anyone with **Admin** on that repository |
| Give a team access to a repository | An **owner**, a **team maintainer**, or anyone with **Admin** on that repository |
| Create a team | Any member, unless the owners have restricted team creation |
| Change base permissions or other organization-wide settings | An organization **owner** (staff) |

### Base member permissions

Every member has a **base permission** that applies to **all of the organization's repositories** unless a team grants them more. Ours is set to **Read**, which means:

- ✅ Clone and read any repository, open issues, comment, and review pull requests.
- ✅ Fork a repository and **send a pull request from the fork** --- this is how anyone without write access contributes changes.
- ✅ Create a new repository from one of our template repositories.
- ❌ **Cannot** push branches to our repositories, and therefore cannot open a pull request from a branch inside one of them (fork first).
- ❌ **Cannot** merge pull requests, apply labels, close or assign issues, or change repository settings and access.

We call these members **base members**: they are ordinary members who haven't been added to a team, so the base permission is all they have. It isn't a lesser kind of membership --- just the starting point before any team is involved. It's a sensible default: it lets people read and discuss everything we do, and contribute changes through forks, without giving them write access to repositories they're not working on.

> **Base permissions do not apply to outside collaborators** --- they only get the access granted to them on the specific repositories they've been added to.

You can review base permissions in the [organization's member privileges settings](https://github.com/organizations/lmu-osc/settings/member_privileges). Teams are how we raise members above this base level: adding someone to a team gives them that team's role on the repositories it covers, which keeps our permissions auditable and makes offboarding a single action.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Setting base permissions for an organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-repository-roles/setting-base-permissions-for-an-organization).

### Adding new members

**Inviting people to the organization is an owner-level action --- in practice, a staff member does it**, so ask one if that isn't you. (The one exception: a team maintainer can add a non-member straight into their own team, which sends the same invitation.) Open the organization's **People** tab, click **Invite Member**, and search by username, full name, or email.

Decide up front whether they belong in a team:

- **Into a team** (the usual case) --- they immediately get that team's role on the repositories it covers.
- **No team** (base member) --- they get base Read only. This is what you want for [commissioned external people](#commissioned-external-people-freelancers-contractors) below.

Unaccepted invites expire after seven days and can be resent. If you don't see the invite option, you don't have owner access --- ask a staff member.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Inviting users to join your organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-membership-in-your-organization/inviting-users-to-join-your-organization) --- then come back here for who goes into which team.

#### Commissioned external people (freelancers, contractors)

For a one-off commission from someone who isn't joining the OSC --- a freelance designer building a template, say:

1. **A staff member invites them as a member**, adding them to no team. Base **Read** is all they need to browse and clone our repositories, and to create a new repository of their own from one of our templates (such as the tutorial template), which they control fully.
2. **We agree the end date up front**, because offboarding them means removing them from the organization entirely.
3. **We don't give them elevated access to our existing repositories.** If the work happens *inside* one of our repositories, use an [outside collaborator](#giving-access-to-a-single-repository-outside-collaborators) with Write on that repository instead.

> **Why not a team?** A team would give a contractor access to *all* of our repositories --- far more than a one-off commission needs.

### Giving access to a single repository (outside collaborators)

For someone who needs one repository and shouldn't be a member, add them as an **outside collaborator** from the repository's **Settings → Collaborators and teams → Add people**. This needs **Admin** on that repository, which both our staff and HiWi teams have. Pick the lowest role that lets them work (usually Write).

- ✅ One repository, one-off work, inside an existing repository of ours.
- ✅ If they need to build something new from one of our templates instead, follow the [commissioned external people](#commissioned-external-people-freelancers-contractors) procedure.
- ❌ If you're adding the same person repeatedly, make them a member instead --- `osc-trusted-members`, or a team of their own --- rather than stacking up per-repository invitations.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Adding outside collaborators to repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-outside-collaborators/adding-outside-collaborators-to-repositories-in-your-organization).

### Member visibility

Membership is **Private** by default, so nobody outside the organization can see it. We **ask members to make theirs Public**, so other members, collaborators, and the community can see who is part of the OSC and who to contact about what. It's optional: change it from **Private** to **Public** on your [organization memberships page](https://github.com/settings/organizations).

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [Publicizing or hiding organization membership](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/organization-membership/publicizing-or-hiding-organization-membership).

### Organization owners

Owners have full control over the organization: managing members and teams, organization-wide settings (base permissions, 2FA requirements), all repositories including private ones --- and deleting the organization.

We grant owner access only to **full-time staff**, not to HiWis or other collaborators, and may restrict it further in future. Being an Owner is what lets someone invite or remove members and change organization-wide settings --- see [Who can do what](#who-can-do-what). If you need something owner-level done --- creating a team, changing org-wide settings, adding an owner --- ask a staff member. Repository admins cannot do these things.

## Security: two-factor authentication (2FA)

We are in the process of **requiring 2FA** for all members. Even if a password is compromised, a second factor stops someone getting into our repositories and code. If you already have 2FA enabled you're all set; if not, set it up before you can access the organization.

We recommend a **TOTP app** (Google Authenticator, 1Password, Duo, Microsoft Authenticator) or the **GitHub Mobile app**. Passkeys and hardware security keys are also good options. **SMS is not recommended** --- codes sent by text can be intercepted, and GitHub advises against it.

Whichever you choose, **save your recovery codes** in your password manager: they're the only way back into your account if you lose your phone.

> **Read the GitHub docs:** [About two-factor authentication](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/about-two-factor-authentication) explains the options and [Configuring two-factor authentication](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/configuring-two-factor-authentication) walks through the setup --- then come back here, and check [Who to ask for help](#who-to-ask-for-help) if you get stuck.

### Who to ask for help

If you run into any of the following, here's who to contact:

| Situation | Who to ask |
|---|---|
| I need to be added to the organization | Any full-time staff member (an organization owner) |
| I need someone else invited to (or removed from) the organization | Any full-time staff member (only owners can do this) |
| I can't access a specific repository | Ask the team that maintains it, or a staff member |
| I need a new team created | You can create one yourself; giving it repository access needs Admin on those repositories, or ask a staff member |
| I'm having trouble with 2FA | Check the [GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa) or ask a staff member |
| I'm not sure where a project lives | Check the organization's Repositories tab, or ask in the relevant Matrix channel |
